p: It is two o'clock in the morning in Yopougon. The street is quiet. The dogs are quiet. The big mango tree in front of the house is quiet. Only one thing in the house is not quiet. It is Aya's phone.

Aya is fifteen years old. She lives in a small blue house with her mother, her little brother Junior and her grandmother, Mamie Akissi. Her room is very small. There is a bed, a table, a chair and a window. On the bed, under a thin blanket, there is a light. It is the light of Aya's phone.
"Just one more video," Aya says to herself. "Just one more."
She watches a girl dancing in Lagos. She watches a cat jumping into a box. She watches a man cooking chicken in a very big pot. She laughs. She types a message to her friend Fatou: "Are you awake?"
Fatou answers in ten seconds. "Of course! Look at this video!"
Aya looks. She laughs again. Then she looks at the time. It is now three o'clock.
"Oh no," she says. "School starts at seven."
She closes her eyes. But her phone makes a little sound. *Ding!* A new message. She opens her eyes. She takes the phone again.
At six o'clock, her mother opens the door.
"Aya! Get up! You are late!"

Aya's mother is called Mariam. She is a tall woman with strong arms and a big laugh. Every morning she goes to the market at Siporex to sell attiéké and fried fish. She works very hard. She does not like it when Aya is late.
"Five more minutes, Maman," Aya says.
"No. Not five minutes. Not one minute. Get up now!"
Aya gets up. Her eyes are red. Her head is heavy. She walks to the bathroom like a zombie. In the mirror, she sees a tired girl with a tired face.
"Who is that?" she asks the mirror. The mirror does not answer.
In the kitchen, her little brother Junior is eating bread with butter. Junior is eight years old. He has a big smile with no front teeth.
"You look terrible," Junior says.
"Thank you, Junior. You are very kind," Aya says.
"Did you sleep with your phone again?"
"Eat your bread."

Mamie Akissi is sitting near the window. She is seventy years old. Her hair is white and short. She wears a long yellow dress and glasses on the end of her nose. Every morning she drinks a cup of hot tea with lemon and listens to the radio.
"Good morning, my daughter," she says to Aya. She always says "my daughter" to Aya, not "my granddaughter."
"Good morning, Mamie."
"You know," Mamie says slowly, "when I was young, we did not have phones. We had the moon. At night we looked at the moon, and then we slept."
"Mamie, the moon does not have videos," Aya says.
Junior laughs so hard that bread falls out of his mouth.
Mamie smiles. "No," she says. "But the moon never kept me awake until three o'clock."
Aya does not answer. She drinks some water, takes her school bag and runs out of the house.
At school, the first class is mathematics. The teacher writes numbers on the board. Many numbers. Aya tries to look at them, but the numbers are dancing. They are dancing like the girl in Lagos.
Her eyes close. Her head goes down. Slowly, slowly, her head touches the table.
"Aya Kouassi!"
She jumps. All the students are looking at her. Some of them are laughing.
"Are you sleeping in my class?" the teacher asks.
"No, sir. I am… thinking."
"Thinking with your eyes closed?"
"It is a new method, sir."
The class laughs again. The teacher does not laugh.
"After class, you will stay and clean the board," he says.
Next to Aya, her best friend Fatou whispers: "A new method? You are crazy!"

Fatou is small and fast and always happy. She has long braids with little gold beads. She and Aya are friends since they were six years old. They know everything about each other. Or almost everything.

At ten o'clock it is break time. All the students go out into the yard. And what do they do? They take out their phones. Everybody. Two hundred students, two hundred phones. Nobody is talking. Nobody is playing. Everybody is looking down.

Aya looks at her phone too. She has forty-two new notifications. She smiles. Then she sees something strange. Near the door of the school, there is a big new poster. Some students are standing in front of it.
"Fatou, what is that?" she asks.
"I don't know. Let's look."
They walk to the poster. It is orange, with big black letters. At the top, there is a picture of a phone in a cage.
Aya reads the first words, and her mouth opens.
"Oh no," she says. "No, no, no."
The poster says:

THE SILENT WEEK CHALLENGE
One week. No social media.
No videos. No games.
Can you do it?
Under the big words there are smaller words. Fatou reads them out loud.

"From Monday to Sunday, students can give their phone to their parents. Phones are only for calling the family. The class with the most students in the challenge wins a trip to Grand-Bassam. Also: an English writing competition. Write a story in English about your family. The best story wins a prize."
"A trip to Grand-Bassam!" says a boy behind them. "The beach! The sea!"
"One week without my phone?" says a girl. "Impossible. I will die."
Aya says nothing. She looks at the picture of the phone in the cage. She thinks about the girl dancing in Lagos, the cat in the box, the forty-two notifications. One week. Seven days. Seven nights.
"It's a joke," she says finally. "Nobody can do that."
"I can," says Fatou.
Aya looks at her friend. "You? You send me videos at three o'clock in the morning."
"Yes, but I want to see the sea," Fatou says. "And you… you need to sleep. Look at your face."
"What is wrong with my face?"
"Nothing. It just looks like a sad avocado."
Aya laughs, but she is a little angry too. "OK," she says. "I bet you cannot do it. You will stop on the first day."
"And I bet *you* cannot do it," Fatou answers. "If you stop before Sunday, you buy me ice cream every day for one month."
"And if *you* stop?"
"Then I buy you ice cream for one month."
They look at each other. They are both smiling, but it is a serious smile.
"Deal," says Aya.
"Deal," says Fatou.
They shake hands.

After school, Aya cleans the board for the mathematics teacher. Then she walks home slowly. The sun is very hot. The road is full of taxis, motorbikes and people. A woman is selling oranges. A man is repairing shoes under an umbrella. Children are playing football with a plastic bottle.

Aya does not see them. She is looking at her phone. She is reading comments under her last photo. Somebody wrote: "Beautiful!" Somebody else wrote: "Where is this?" She answers the comments while she walks.
She does not see the hole in the road.
*Boom!* Her foot goes into the hole. She falls. Her bag falls. Her phone flies into the air and lands in the dust.
"Aïe!" she cries.
An old man selling peanuts comes to help her.
"My daughter, are you OK?"
"Yes, yes, I am OK." Her knee is red, but it is not serious. She picks up her phone. The screen has a new line, a small crack, from one corner to the other.
"Look at the road when you walk," the old man says kindly. "The road is not in your phone."
Aya feels her face become hot. "Thank you, sir," she says quietly.
At home, Maman is not back from the market. Junior is doing his homework at the table. Mamie Akissi is in the yard, sitting on her small wooden chair, cutting okra for the sauce.
"What happened to your knee?" Mamie asks.
"Nothing. I fell."
"You fell? Why?"
Aya does not want to answer. But Mamie looks at her over her glasses, and Mamie always knows.
"I was looking at my phone," Aya says.
Mamie nods. She does not say anything. She just cuts the okra. Cut, cut, cut.
Aya sits down next to her. "Mamie, at school there is a challenge. One week without social media. If our class wins, we go to Grand-Bassam."
Mamie stops cutting. She puts down the knife. For a moment, her eyes look very far away.
"Grand-Bassam," she says softly. "I know Grand-Bassam very well."
"You do?"
"Oh yes. A long time ago. Before your mother was born." Mamie smiles a strange little smile. "So. Will you do this challenge?"
"I don't know. One week is very long."
"One week is not long," says Mamie. "When I was your age, I waited three months for one letter."
"Three months? For a letter? Why?"
Mamie picks up the knife again. Cut, cut, cut.
"That is a story for another day," she says.
That night, Aya lies on her bed. The house is quiet. She holds her phone with the broken screen. Through the crack, she sees her messages, her videos, her photos.
She thinks about Fatou. She thinks about the ice cream. She thinks about the old man and the hole in the road. She thinks about Mamie's strange little smile.
At eleven o'clock, she does something she never did before. She stands up, opens the door very quietly and walks to Mamie's room. The light is still on. Mamie is reading a book.
"Mamie," Aya says. "Can you keep my phone? Until Sunday?"
Mamie takes off her glasses. She looks at Aya for a long time. Then she holds out her hand.
Aya gives her the phone. Her hand does not want to let it go. But she lets it go.
"Good night, my daughter," says Mamie. "Look at the moon tonight."
On Monday morning, Aya wakes up at six o'clock. Nobody calls her. Nobody shouts. She just opens her eyes, and she is awake.

It is a strange feeling. Her head is not heavy. Her eyes are not red. Outside, a bird is singing in the mango tree. She never heard this bird before. Maybe it sings every morning, she thinks. Maybe I never listened.
Her hand moves to the table next to the bed. It is looking for the phone. Of course, the phone is not there. Her hand stops in the air, like a bird that does not know where to land.
"OK," Aya says to herself. "Day one."
In the kitchen, Maman is putting on her shoes. She looks surprised.
"You are up? Before me? Are you sick?"
"No, Maman. I slept."
"You slept," Maman repeats. She looks at Mamie. Mamie drinks her tea and says nothing. But her eyes are smiling.
At school, it is a very strange day. In Aya's class there are forty students. Twenty-two of them are in the challenge. At break time, they do not know what to do with their hands.
"What do people do without phones?" asks a boy called Ibrahim. He is standing in the middle of the yard, looking at his empty hands.
"I think they talk," says Fatou.
"Talk about what?"
"I don't know. Things."

So they talk. At first it is difficult. There are long silences. But then Ibrahim tells a story about his uncle's goat that ate a whole shirt. Everybody laughs. Then a girl called Mireille tells a story about her grandmother who speaks to her plants. Then another story. And another. When the bell rings, Aya is surprised. Break time is finished already?
During the English class, the teacher, Madame Diallo, talks about the writing competition.
"Your story must be about your family," she says. "It can be true or it can be imagined. But it must be in English. Use simple words. Use your heart."
"Madame, my English is very bad," says Ibrahim.
"Then this is a good chance to make it better," says Madame Diallo. "Every great writer started with bad sentences."

Aya writes in her notebook: *Story about my family.* Then she looks at the words for a long time. What can she write? Her family is normal. Maman sells fish. Junior loses his teeth. Mamie drinks tea. There is no story.
After school, Aya walks home. And this time, she sees the road.

She sees the woman with the oranges. The woman has a baby on her back, and the baby is sleeping with its mouth open. She sees the man repairing shoes. He is singing an old song while he works. She sees the children with the plastic bottle. One of them scores a goal and runs around with his shirt on his head.
She sees the old man with the peanuts.
"Hello, sir," she says.
He looks at her. Then he remembers. "Ah! The girl who fell! How is your knee?"
"It's fine. Thank you."
"Today you are looking at the road," he says, smiling.
"Today I am looking at everything," says Aya.
He gives her a small bag of peanuts. "A present," he says. "For a girl with open eyes."
At home, the afternoon is long. Very long. Aya does her homework. That takes forty minutes. Then she sits on the bed. She looks at the wall. The wall looks at her.
Usually, at this time, she is watching videos. Now there is only the wall.
She goes to the kitchen. Junior is drawing a picture of a dinosaur.
"What are you doing?" she asks.
"Drawing. You want to draw?"
"I don't know how to draw."
"Everybody knows how to draw," says Junior. "You take a pencil and you make lines."
So Aya sits down and draws. She draws a dinosaur too. It looks like a potato with legs. Junior looks at it seriously.
"It's very bad," he says.
"Thank you, Junior."
"But it's funny. I like it."
They draw for one hour. They draw a dinosaur family, a dinosaur school and a dinosaur who sells attiéké at the market. They laugh so much that Mamie comes to see what is happening.
When Maman comes home, she finds her two children on the floor, surrounded by drawings.
"What is this?" she asks.
"The dinosaur market," says Junior. "This one is you."
Maman looks at the drawing of a big green dinosaur with a basket of fish on its head. For a moment, nobody moves. Then Maman laughs her big laugh, the laugh that fills the whole house.
"I am more beautiful than that!" she says.
That evening, they eat together. All four of them, at the same table, at the same time. Aya realizes it is the first time in many weeks.
At night, Aya cannot sleep. Not because of a phone. Because of a question.
What did Mamie mean? Three months for one letter?
She gets up and walks to the kitchen to drink some water. Mamie's door is a little open. There is no light. Mamie is sleeping.
But on the floor, near the door, there is something. Aya bends down. It is an old envelope, very old, yellow like dry leaves. Maybe it fell from a book.
On the envelope, in beautiful blue handwriting, there is a name and an address:

*Miss Akissi Yao*
*Hôtel de la Plage*
*Grand-Bassam, Ivory Coast*
And in the corner, there is a stamp with the face of a queen.
In the morning, Aya gives the envelope to Mamie.
"I found this on the floor near your door," she says. "Who is Miss Akissi Yao?"
Mamie takes the envelope with both hands, very carefully, like a bird with a broken wing. She looks at it for a long time.
"Akissi Yao," she says. "That was me. Yao was my name before I married your grandfather."
"And the Hôtel de la Plage? In Grand-Bassam?"
"I worked there. When I was eighteen."
Aya sits down next to her. "Mamie, you never told me that."
"You never asked," says Mamie. It is not an angry answer. It is a true answer.

Aya feels something strange in her chest. All her life, Mamie was just Mamie. The woman with the tea and the radio and the yellow dress. She never thought Mamie was eighteen once. That Mamie had a life, a job, secrets.
"Who sent you this letter?" Aya asks. "There is a queen on the stamp."
Mamie stands up slowly. "Come," she says. "I will show you."

Mamie's room is small and clean. It smells of soap and old wood. There is a bed with a white sheet, a cupboard and a big photo of Grandfather on the wall. Grandfather died when Aya was five. In the photo he is wearing a suit and a serious face.
Mamie opens the cupboard. Under her dresses, at the bottom, there is a wooden box. It is dark brown, with flowers carved on the top. Mamie gives it to Aya.
"Open it."

Inside the box there are letters. Many letters. Maybe fifty. Some are white, some are yellow, some are blue. They are tied together with a red ribbon. All of them have the same stamp with the queen. All of them have the same beautiful blue handwriting.
"They are from England," says Mamie. "From my friend Margaret."
"Margaret?"
Mamie sits on the bed. She takes off her glasses and cleans them with her dress. Aya knows this movement. Mamie does it when she is going to tell a long story.

"In 1975," Mamie begins, "I was a young woman. I worked at the Hôtel de la Plage. I cleaned the rooms, I carried the towels, I served breakfast. One day, a family arrived from England. A father, a mother and a girl. The girl was eighteen, like me. Her name was Margaret."
"Did you speak English?"

Mamie laughs. "Not one word! And Margaret did not speak one word of French. But every morning I brought her breakfast, and every morning she said 'thank you' and I said 'merci.' Then she said 'merci' and I said 'thank you.' And we laughed."
"That's all?"

"That was the beginning. Her family stayed six weeks. Every day, after my work, Margaret and I walked on the beach. She taught me English words. *Sea. Sand. Sun. Friend.* I taught her French words. *Mer. Sable. Soleil. Amie.* We drew pictures in the sand when we did not know the words."
Aya imagines it. Two girls on a beach, drawing in the sand. No phones. No videos. Just the sea and the words.
"And then?"

"Then she went back to England. And she wrote to me. And I wrote to her. With a dictionary, very slowly, one word, then another word. A letter took one month to go to England and one month to come back. Sometimes three months, if the boat was slow." Mamie touches the letters. "Five years, we wrote to each other. Five years."
"Can I read them?"
Mamie hesitates. Then she nods. "They are in English. You will need your dictionary."
That evening, Aya sits at the kitchen table with the first letter and her big English–French dictionary. Junior sits next to her. He cannot read English, but he wants to help.
The paper is thin and soft. The handwriting is round and beautiful. Aya reads the first line very slowly.
*Dear Akissi,*
"Dear," she says. "That's easy. *Cher. Chère.*"
*I am home in London now. It is cold and grey. I miss the sun. I miss the sea. I miss you, my friend.*
Aya looks for "miss" in the dictionary. There are many meanings. She finds the right one: *manquer.* I miss you. *Tu me manques.*
She reads the sentence again. *I miss you, my friend.* Something warm moves in her chest.
"What does it say?" asks Junior.
"It says that Margaret was sad without Mamie."
"Why? Was Mamie funny?"
"I think," Aya says slowly, "that Mamie was her best friend."

She continues. It takes her one hour to read one letter. Her notebook is full of new words: *grey, to miss, weather, umbrella, lonely, to hope.* Her head is tired, but it is a good tired. Not like the tired of three o'clock in the morning. It is the tired of a person who learned something.
When she goes to bed, she does not think about her phone. Not even one time. She thinks about a girl in London, in the rain, writing to a girl in Grand-Bassam, in the sun.
On Wednesday, Aya has an idea.
At break time, she tells Fatou about the box, the letters and Margaret. Fatou listens with her mouth open.
"Your grandmother had an English best friend? In 1975? That's like a film!"
"I know. And I want to read all the letters. But it is very slow. One letter takes me one hour."
"Then we read them together," says Fatou. "Two heads are better than one."
"You want to help?"
"Of course! I have no phone. I have nothing to do. I am so bored that yesterday I cleaned my room. *Cleaned my room,* Aya! My mother almost cried."

So every afternoon after school, Fatou comes to Aya's house. They sit under the mango tree with the letters, the dictionary and two notebooks. Junior sits with them and draws pictures of the words. When they find the word *umbrella*, he draws an umbrella. When they find *snow*, he draws a snowman, but he has never seen snow, so it looks like a big white yam with eyes.
They make a game. Every day, they choose one new English word. The "word of the day." They must use it ten times before night.
On Wednesday the word is *weather*.
"How is the weather today?" Aya asks Maman when she comes home.
"Hot," says Maman. "Like every day. Why are you speaking English to me?"
"How is the weather in your heart, Maman?"
Maman puts down her basket and looks at her daughter. "My heart is tired, but happy," she says in French. "Because my children are not looking at their phones."
On Thursday the word is *brave*.
On Friday the word is *together*.
The letters tell a story. Aya and Fatou put them in order by date, and slowly the story appears, like a photo in old chemical water.

In the first letters, Margaret talks about London. The rain, the red buses, her work in a bookshop. She asks many questions. *What do you eat in the morning? What songs do you like? Is the sea still blue?*

Mamie's answers are not in the box, of course. They are in England. But Aya can imagine them from Margaret's replies. *You eat fish in the morning? How wonderful! Thank you for the song. I sang it to my mother and she laughed.*

In the middle letters, the two young women grow up. Margaret writes about a man called Peter who works at the bank. *He is very shy. He always brings me flowers but he never says anything.* In 1977, she writes: *I am going to marry Peter! I wish you could come to the wedding. I will wear a white dress and think of you.*
Fatou sighs. "This is better than any video."
In another letter, Margaret writes: *You are getting married too! Kouamé sounds like a good man. Tell him he is very lucky.*
"Kouamé," says Aya. "That's Grandfather."
They look at the photo of Grandfather in their imagination: the suit, the serious face. Was he young once too? Did he bring flowers?
On Friday evening, they arrive at the last letters. The dates are 1979. Margaret's handwriting is faster now, a little nervous.
*Dearest Akissi,*

*I have wonderful news. I am going to have a baby! Peter is so happy he cannot sleep. If it is a girl, maybe one day our daughters will be friends, like us. Can you imagine? Your daughter and my daughter, walking on the beach at Grand-Bassam.*

*Let's make a promise. When our daughters are grown, we will meet again. At the Hôtel de la Plage. On the beach. Under the old palm tree, the one that leans towards the sea. Do you remember it? We drew our names in the sand there.*
*Promise me.*

*Your friend forever,*
*Margaret*
Aya and Fatou look at each other.
"Is that the last one?" asks Fatou.
Aya looks in the box. She shakes it. She looks under the ribbon. There is nothing else.
"That's the last one," she says.
"But… what happened? Did they meet? Did Margaret have a girl? Did your grandmother have…"
Aya stops. *Your daughter and my daughter.* In 1979, Mamie had a baby too. A girl.
That girl was Maman.
On Saturday there is no school. Maman needs help at the market, so Aya goes with her. They leave the house at five o'clock in the morning, when the sky is still dark blue.

The Siporex market is already awake. It is the loudest place in the world. Women are shouting prices. Men are carrying big bags of rice on their heads. Motorbikes are honking. Radios are playing three different songs at the same time. There are smells everywhere: fried fish, ripe mangoes, hot oil, onions, smoke, flowers.
Maman's place is a small wooden table under a blue umbrella. Aya helps her put out the attiéké, the fried fish, the hot pepper sauce and the little plastic bags.
"Two hundred francs for a small bag. Five hundred for a big one with fish," Maman explains. "Smile at the customers. Count the money two times."
Before, Aya hated the market. It was hot and noisy, and there was no time to look at her phone. But today, without her phone, she looks at the people. And the people are interesting.

There is a woman who buys attiéké every day for her twelve children. There is a young policeman who always asks for extra sauce and says it is "for his mother." There is a very old man who pays with coins from 1990 and tells stories about the war.
At ten o'clock, the sun is hot and the market is full. Then Aya hears a voice. A voice speaking English.
"Excuse me… excuse me… do you speak English?"

A woman is standing in the middle of the market. She is white, maybe thirty-five years old, with red hair in a ponytail and a big camera around her neck. Her face is red from the sun. She is holding a piece of paper and looking around with lost eyes.
Nobody answers her. The market women look at her and continue shouting their prices. A boy tries to sell her a phone charger.
"Excuse me, please. Does anybody speak English?"
Aya's heart starts to beat very fast. *I speak English,* she thinks. *A little. Maybe. Not really.*
"Maman," she whispers. "That woman needs help."
"Then help her," says Maman, cutting a fish.
"But my English is not very good."
Maman stops cutting. She looks at her daughter. "Aya. All week you read letters in English. All week you speak English to me in my own kitchen. Go."
Aya takes a deep breath. She walks to the woman. Her legs feel like water.
"Hello," she says. "Can I… help you?"
The woman turns around. Her whole face opens like a window.
"Oh! Thank goodness! Yes, please. I'm looking for this place." She shows the piece of paper. There is an address written on it in pencil.
Aya reads it. *Rue des Jardins, Yopougon. Near the big mango tree. Blue house.*
Aya reads it again. And again.
"I think I know this street," she says slowly. "It is… near my house."
"Really? That's wonderful! I've been looking for two hours. Every taxi takes me to a different place."
"Why… why do you look for this house?" Aya asks. She knows her grammar is not perfect, but the woman understands.

"I'm looking for someone. An old friend of my family. My grandmother wrote this address many, many years ago. I don't even know if the person still lives there." The woman laughs nervously. "It's a crazy story. I'm sorry. My name is Sarah, by the way."
"I am Aya."
"Nice to meet you, Aya." Sarah shakes her hand. Then she looks at her watch. "Oh no. I'm late. I have a meeting at my hotel in thirty minutes. Can I come back tomorrow? Can you show me the street?"
"Yes. OK. Tomorrow."
"Where can I find you?"
"Here. At this table. My mother sells attiéké."
"Tomorrow, then! Thank you so much, Aya. Your English is very good."
And she disappears into the crowd, with her red hair and her big camera.
Aya walks back to the table. Her heart is still beating fast. Maman looks at her.
"So?"
"I spoke English, Maman. Really. With an English woman. And she understood me!"
Maman smiles her biggest smile. She gives Aya a piece of fried fish. "This is for my daughter, the translator," she says.
Aya eats the fish. It is the best fish of her life.

But all afternoon, a little question walks around in her head like an ant. *A blue house. Near the big mango tree. Rue des Jardins.* There are many blue houses in Yopougon. There are many mango trees.
But there is only one blue house with a mango tree on Rue des Jardins.
And it is her house.
That evening, Aya runs to Fatou's house. She wants to tell her everything about Sarah. But when she arrives, Fatou is sitting alone on the steps in front of her door. Her face is wet.
"Fatou? What's wrong?"
Fatou wipes her eyes quickly. "Nothing. Dust in my eyes."
"Fatou."
Fatou looks at the ground. Through the window, Aya hears voices. A man's voice and a woman's voice. They are shouting. Something falls and breaks.
Aya sits down next to her friend. She says nothing. She just sits there.
For a long time, they listen to the voices. Then the voices stop. A door closes. A car starts and drives away.
"My father," says Fatou quietly. "He goes away when they fight. Sometimes he comes back the next day. Sometimes after three days."
"How long… how long has this been happening?"

"Since last year." Fatou plays with the gold beads in her braids. "Every night, when they start to fight, I put my headphones on and I watch videos. Funny videos. Very loud. Until three o'clock in the morning. Then I don't hear anything."
Aya feels something cold in her stomach. All those messages at three o'clock in the morning. *Are you awake? Look at this video!* She thought Fatou was just having fun. She never asked why.
"Why didn't you tell me?" she asks.
"I don't know. It's embarrassing. Everybody's parents are fine. Your mother laughs all the time."
"My father left when Junior was a baby," Aya says. "You know that."
"Yes, but your house is happy."
"It's not always happy. We just… don't talk about the sad things."
Fatou laughs a small, wet laugh. "This week is terrible. Without my phone, I hear everything. Every word. Every door."
Aya takes her friend's hand. It is the hand of the six-year-old girl who shared her biscuits on the first day of school. The hand of the girl who dared her to do the challenge.
"Then this week," Aya says, "you don't stay here at night. You come to my house."
"Your mother won't want…"
"My mother," says Aya, "will make you eat so much attiéké that you can't walk."
Maman does not ask many questions. She looks at Fatou's red eyes, and she understands. She puts a mattress in Aya's room and gives Fatou a clean pillow that smells of soap.
"Stay as long as you want, my daughter," she says. Like Mamie, she says "my daughter" to everybody.
That night, the two girls lie in the dark room. There is no light from a phone. Only the moon, coming through the window.
"Aya?"
"Mm?"
"Can I tell you something stupid?"
"Always."
"I think the silence is less scary when somebody is next to you."
Aya looks at the moon. She thinks of Mamie. *When I was young, we did not have phones. We had the moon.*
"It's not stupid," she says. "It's the most intelligent thing you ever said."
"Hey!"
They laugh in the dark, trying to be quiet, which makes them laugh more. From the other room, Junior shouts: "Some people are trying to sleep!" And that makes them laugh even more.
Then, slowly, the laughing stops. And Aya tells Fatou about the red-haired woman, the piece of paper, the blue house and the mango tree.
Fatou sits up. "Wait. She is looking for your house? Who is she looking for?"
"I don't know. She said 'an old friend of my family.' Her grandmother wrote the address many years ago."
They look at each other in the moonlight. The same idea arrives in both their heads at the same time.
"Margaret," they whisper together.
At midnight, the storm arrives.

First there is wind. The mango tree moves and cries. The windows shake. Then there is thunder, so loud that Junior runs into Aya's room with his blanket. Then the rain comes. Not normal rain. A wall of water, like the sky is falling.
And then, *click*, the electricity goes off.
"Aya!" Junior grabs her arm in the dark. "I can't see anything!"
"It's OK, Junior. It's just a power cut."
"Where is your phone? We need the light!"
Aya almost laughs. "Mamie has my phone. Remember?"
A small yellow light appears in the corridor. It is Mamie, with a candle in her hand. Behind her is Maman, with another candle.
"Everybody in the kitchen," says Mamie. "When there is a storm, we stay together."

So they all sit in the kitchen: Mamie, Maman, Junior, Aya and Fatou. The two candles make long shadows on the walls. Outside, the rain is shouting. Inside, it is warm and orange and strangely peaceful.
"When I was a child," says Maman, "and there was a power cut, Mamie told us stories."
Junior looks at his grandmother with big eyes. "Mamie, tell a story!"
Mamie looks at Aya. Aya looks at Mamie. Then Aya says:
"Tell us about Margaret. Please. Tell us why the letters stopped."
Maman looks surprised. "Margaret? Who is Margaret?"
"You don't know?" says Aya.
"I know there was a friend in England. A long time ago. Mamie never talked about it."
Mamie is quiet for a long moment. The candle moves on her face. Then she takes off her glasses and cleans them with her dress. The long-story movement.

"In 1979," she begins, "I was pregnant with you, Mariam. Margaret was pregnant too. We were so happy. We wrote that our daughters will be friends. We made a promise to meet again in Grand-Bassam, under the old palm tree, when our daughters were grown."
"What happened?" asks Fatou softly.

"Life happened. Your grandfather got a new job in Abidjan. We moved here, to this blue house. The Hôtel de la Plage closed the same year. I wrote to Margaret. I gave her this new address. Rue des Jardins, the blue house, near the big mango tree. I wrote it very clearly."
"And she answered?" asks Junior.
Mamie shakes her head slowly. "I waited. One month. Three months. Six months. One year. Nothing. I wrote again. Nothing. I wrote five letters. No answer."
"Maybe the letters were lost," says Aya.

"Maybe. Or maybe she was busy with her baby. With her new life. Maybe she forgot me." Mamie puts her glasses back on. "After two years, I stopped writing. I put her letters in the box, and I put the box under my dresses. And I did not open it for forty years."
In the kitchen, nobody speaks. Only the rain.
Then Maman takes her mother's hand. "Maman," she says, "why didn't you tell me?"
"Because it was sad. And sad things, we keep inside."
Aya thinks about Fatou on the steps. About her own father who left. About all the sad things that everybody keeps inside, behind smiles and screens and funny videos.
"Mamie," she says. "I don't think Margaret forgot you."
"How do you know?"

Aya takes a deep breath. And she tells them about the market. About the woman with red hair and the big camera. About the piece of paper with the address in pencil. *Rue des Jardins. Near the big mango tree. Blue house.* About the words: *My grandmother wrote this address many, many years ago.*
When she finishes, Mamie's hand is shaking. The candle is shaking too.
"What was her name?" Mamie asks. Her voice is very small.
"Sarah."
"Sarah," Mamie repeats. She says it like a word in a foreign language that she is trying to understand.
"She will come back tomorrow," says Aya. "To the market. I promised to show her the way."
Mamie closes her eyes. Two tears run down her face, slowly, into the lines of her old skin. But she is smiling. It is the strange little smile from the day Aya first said *Grand-Bassam*.
"Forty years," she says. "And now one day. Only one more day."
Outside, the storm is getting worse. The wind is pulling the leaves off the mango tree. Somewhere, something metal falls with a loud noise.

Nobody can sleep. So they stay in the kitchen and talk. Mamie tells stories about the Hôtel de la Plage. Maman tells stories about her childhood. Fatou tells funny stories about her cousins. Junior falls asleep with his head on the table.
At four o'clock in the morning, the rain stops. Aya looks out of the window. The street is a river. The water is up to the knees of the mango tree.
"Maman," she says. "Will the market be open tomorrow?"
Maman looks at the river in the street. She does not answer.
On Sunday morning, the Siporex market is under water.

Aya and Maman walk there anyway, with their shoes in their hands and the brown water up to their ankles. Many tables are broken. Umbrellas are lying in the mud. The market women are cleaning, crying, laughing, shouting, all at the same time. Nobody is selling anything today.
Maman's table is still there, but the blue umbrella is gone. The wind took it.
"We cannot sell today," says Maman. "Maybe tomorrow. Maybe Tuesday."
Aya does not listen. She is looking everywhere. Left, right, behind the broken tables, near the road. She is looking for red hair and a big camera.
She waits one hour. Two hours. Three hours. The sun comes out and the water slowly goes down. Many people pass. Taxis, motorbikes, children, a man with a goat. But no red hair. No camera.
"She's not coming," Aya says finally.
"Maybe she came early," says Maman gently. "Maybe she saw the water and went back to her hotel."

"Which hotel? I don't know her hotel. I don't know her family name. I don't know anything!" Aya kicks a plastic bottle. It flies into the mud. "I only know 'Sarah.' Do you know how many Sarahs there are in the world?"
Maman puts her arm around her daughter's shoulders. Her arm is strong and warm and smells of fish and soap.
"Come," she says. "Let's go home."

At home, Mamie is sitting by the window. She is wearing her best dress, the blue one with gold flowers, the one she wears for weddings and funerals. When she sees Aya and Maman come in alone, she does not ask anything. She just nods and looks back at the window.
Aya cannot look at her. She goes to her room and closes the door.
She lies on her bed. She is so angry. Angry at the storm. Angry at herself. Why didn't she ask Sarah's family name? Why didn't she ask the name of her hotel? Why didn't she take her phone number?
*Phone number.* Aya sits up.

It is Sunday. The last day of the Silent Week. At midnight, she can have her phone back. With her phone, she can search. She can look on social media for "Sarah, red hair, Abidjan, camera." She can post a message: *Looking for an English woman called Sarah.* Maybe somebody knows her. Maybe…
She looks at the clock. It is three o'clock in the afternoon. Nine more hours.
Then she thinks: *Mamie waited forty years.*

That evening, Aya does not wait for midnight. She sits at the kitchen table with a clean notebook. Madame Diallo said the story must be about your family. True or imagined. In English. Simple words. With your heart.
She knows what to write now.

She writes slowly. She uses the dictionary for many words. She makes mistakes and crosses them out. Fatou sits next to her and helps with the grammar. Junior draws pictures for every page. Even Maman, who speaks only a little English, says: "Write that she was the most beautiful girl in Grand-Bassam. It's true. Everybody says so."
Mamie does not help. She sits by the window and watches the street. But sometimes, when Aya reads a sentence out loud, she smiles.
The story is called *Two Girls on a Beach*.
It starts like this:

*In 1975, in a hotel in Grand-Bassam, there was a girl who did not speak English, and a girl who did not speak French. Every morning one of them said "thank you" and the other said "merci." This is how a friendship started that lasted forty years, even when the letters stopped.*
At eleven o'clock, Aya writes the last sentence. She reads the whole story to her family. When she finishes, the kitchen is very quiet.
Then Mamie stands up, walks to her daughter's daughter and kisses her on the forehead.
"It's beautiful," she says. "But the ending is sad."
"I don't know the ending," says Aya. "Nobody knows the ending."
"Then maybe," says Mamie, "the story is not finished."
At midnight, Mamie gives Aya her phone. Seven days. One hundred and sixty-eight hours. She did it.
Aya holds the phone in her hand. She turns it on. The screen with the crack lights up. *Ding! Ding! Ding! Ding!* Two hundred and twelve notifications.
She looks at them for a long time.
Then she turns the phone off again, puts it on the table, and goes to sleep.
On Monday, the whole school is in the yard for the results. Two hundred students in the sun. This time, some of them have their phones in their hands again. But many of them don't. They are talking.
The director stands on a small stage with a microphone. Next to him is Madame Diallo, with a pile of papers.

"Good morning, students," says the director. "Last week, many of you tried the Silent Week challenge. Some of you stopped after one day." Some students laugh. "Some of you stopped after one hour." More students laugh. Ibrahim looks at the ground. "But some of you did it. Seven days. And one class did it better than all the others."
He looks at his paper.
"In class Troisième B, thirty-one students out of forty finished the challenge. Troisième B, you are going to Grand-Bassam on Saturday!"
The yard explodes. Aya's class jumps and shouts and hugs. Ibrahim lifts Fatou into the air. Fatou screams. Mireille cries. Even the mathematics teacher smiles, a little.
"Fatou!" says Aya. "You did it! Seven days!"
"*We* did it," says Fatou. "So nobody buys ice cream for one month."
"Or," says Aya, "we both buy ice cream for each other."
"That's the best deal in history."
Then Madame Diallo takes the microphone.

"And now, the English writing competition. We received fifty-three stories. Some were funny. Some were sad. Some were… very creative." She looks at Ibrahim. Everybody knows his story was about his uncle's goat. "But one story touched all the teachers. It is a true story, about a grandmother and a friendship. The title is *Two Girls on a Beach*. The winner is… Aya Kouassi!"
Aya cannot move. Fatou pushes her. "Go! Go!"
She walks to the stage. Her legs are water again, like at the market. Madame Diallo gives her a certificate and a book: a big English dictionary with a blue cover.
"Will you read the beginning for us?" Madame Diallo asks.
Aya looks at two hundred faces. Two hundred students who usually look at screens. Now they are looking at her.
She takes the microphone. Her voice shakes a little at the start. Then it becomes stronger.
"*In 1975, in a hotel in Grand-Bassam, there was a girl who did not speak English, and a girl who did not speak French…*"
She reads the whole first page. When she stops, there is a moment of silence. Then the students clap. Loud. Long.
In the crowd, Aya sees Fatou crying and laughing. She sees Ibrahim clapping with his hands over his head. And at the gate of the school, she sees someone she did not expect.
Mamie. In her blue dress with gold flowers. Maman brought her on the back of a moto-taxi, and she is standing there, holding the gate with one hand and her heart with the other.
After the ceremony, Madame Diallo comes to talk to Mamie.
"Madame, your granddaughter wrote a beautiful story. Is it really true?"
"Every word," says Mamie. "Except one thing."
"What thing?"
"She wrote that I was the most beautiful girl in Grand-Bassam." Mamie smiles. "That is not true. Margaret was also very beautiful."
Madame Diallo laughs. Then she becomes serious. "Aya told me about the English woman at the market. Sarah. I'm so sorry she didn't come back."
"Life is long," says Mamie. "Sometimes it is slow. But it is long."
Madame Diallo thinks for a moment. "On Saturday, the class goes to Grand-Bassam. We need some adults to help with the children. Would you like to come with us, Madame?"
Mamie's eyes open wide behind her glasses. "To Grand-Bassam? Me?"
"You know the town better than all of us," says Madame Diallo. "And maybe you can show the students the old Hôtel de la Plage."
Mamie looks at Aya. Aya nods so hard that her head almost falls off.
"Yes," says Mamie. "Yes. After so many years, I will go back."

That night, Aya turns on her phone for the first time since Sunday. She reads her messages. She looks at some photos. It is nice, but it is not the same. After twenty minutes, she is bored. She feels like she is eating a whole bag of sweets: nice at the start, then a little sick.
She puts the phone on the table, screen down.
Then she goes to Mamie's room. Mamie is awake, sitting on her bed with the wooden box open on her knees. She is reading the last letter.
*Under the old palm tree, the one that leans towards the sea.*
"Do you think the palm tree is still there?" Aya asks.
"Palm trees live a long time," says Mamie. "Longer than promises, sometimes. Shorter than friendships."

On Saturday, the school bus leaves Yopougon at seven o'clock in the morning. It is an old yellow bus with no air conditioning and a driver who sings every song on the radio. Forty students, three teachers, two parents and one grandmother.
The students sing too. They sing loud and badly. Mamie sits at the front, next to Madame Diallo, holding a small bag on her knees. Inside the bag there is the wooden box.
The road goes along the lagoon. Then the city becomes smaller, the trees become bigger, and the air starts to smell of salt.
"The sea!" shouts Junior. Madame Diallo let him come too, because he promised to be very, very good. He is not very, very good. He is jumping on his seat.
Aya looks out of the window. And there it is. Blue. Enormous. Moving. Shining. The sea.
She has seen it in a thousand videos. But it is different in real life. In real life, it is bigger than the screen. In real life, it has a sound, a smell, a wind.

Grand-Bassam is an old town, with old houses in many colors: yellow, pink, blue, green. Some houses are beautiful. Some houses are falling down, with trees growing through the windows. Mamie walks slowly in the streets, looking at everything.

"This was the post office," she says, pointing at a yellow building. "I posted my letters here. And this was a little shop where I bought bread. The woman was called Tantie Rose. She gave me extra bread because I was thin."
Then they arrive at a long white building near the beach. The paint is old. The windows are broken. There is a sign, but most of the letters are gone. Aya can only read: *HÔT L DE LA PL GE*.
Mamie stops. For a long time, she does not move.
"Is it here?" Aya asks softly.
Mamie nods. "I carried towels up those stairs. Every day. Six days a week. One thousand towels."
The students are quiet now. Even Junior. They look at the old hotel, and then they look at the old woman, and somehow they understand.
"Where is the palm tree?" asks Fatou.
Mamie turns towards the beach. She walks. Aya walks next to her and holds her arm, because the sand is soft and Mamie's legs are seventy years old.
The beach is long and golden. The waves are big and white. There are many palm trees. Tall ones, small ones, straight ones.
And one that leans towards the sea.
It is old now. Its trunk is grey and curved like a question mark. But it is there. It is still there.
Mamie walks to the palm tree. She puts her hand on the trunk, like you put your hand on the shoulder of an old friend.
"Hello," she says to the tree. "I came back."
Aya stands a few steps behind. She does not want to disturb this moment. She looks at the sea, at the waves, at the sky.
And then she sees something.
Further along the beach, a woman is taking photos of the sea. She has a big camera. And red hair in a ponytail.
Aya's heart stops. Then it starts again, very fast.
"Sarah?" she whispers. Then louder: "SARAH!"
The woman turns. She looks at Aya. For a second, she does not understand. Then her whole face opens like a window, exactly like at the market.
"Aya? Aya from the market?"
Aya runs. She runs on the soft sand, she falls, she gets up, she runs again. Sarah runs too. They meet in the middle of the beach, out of breath.

"I came back on Sunday," Sarah says quickly. "I swear I came back! But the market was under water, and there was nobody, and I didn't know your name, your family name, anything. And on Tuesday I tried again, and the table was there but a different woman was selling, and she said your mother was at home because she was sick…"
"Maman had a fever," says Aya. "After the storm."

"I was so sad," says Sarah. "I'm flying back to London tomorrow. I came here today because… because this was a special place for my grandmother. She told me about this beach all my life. I wanted to take a photo of a tree. A very old palm tree. She said it leans towards the sea."
Aya cannot speak. She just turns around and points.
Under the old palm tree, a small woman in a blue dress with gold flowers is standing with her hand on the trunk.
Sarah looks at her. She looks at the tree. She looks at Aya.
"Is that…?"
"That's my grandmother," says Aya. "Her name is Akissi."
Sarah puts her hand on her mouth. Her camera hangs on her neck, forgotten.
"Akissi Yao," she says. "From the letters."
Sarah walks to the palm tree very slowly, like a person walking into a church.

Mamie turns around. She sees the red hair. She sees the face. And Aya sees something incredible: Mamie's face becomes young. Just for a second. Like the girl of eighteen in the hotel is looking through the eyes of the old woman.
"You have her eyes," Mamie says in French. Then, slowly, carefully, in English: "You… have… Margaret's eyes."
Sarah begins to cry. "Everybody says that," she laughs through her tears. "I'm Sarah. Margaret is my grandmother."
"*Is,*" Mamie repeats. Her voice shakes. "You said *is*. Not *was*."

"She's alive! She's seventy years old. She lives in London, in a little house with a garden. She grows tomatoes and she complains about the rain." Sarah takes Mamie's hands. "And she talks about you all the time. Akissi. Her friend in Africa. The friend she lost."
"She lost me?" says Mamie. "But she stopped writing. In 1979. I wrote five letters. No answer."

Sarah shakes her head. "No. No, no. She wrote to you! Many times! But all her letters came back with a stamp: *Unknown address*. The hotel was closed. She never received your new address. She thought… she thought you moved away and forgot her."
Mamie closes her eyes. For forty years, two women in two countries thought the same sad thing. *She forgot me.* And it was never true.
"The letters," says Aya. "Your five letters, Mamie. With the new address. Maybe they were lost. Maybe a boat. Maybe a post office. Maybe a storm."
"Maybe," says Mamie. She opens her eyes. They are wet, but they are shining. "It doesn't matter now."
Sarah takes something out of her bag. It is an old envelope, white, with a stamp of the Ivory Coast.

"This is the only letter she ever received from you after you moved," Sarah says. "It arrived in 1990. Eleven years late. The envelope was damaged by water, and the address on the back was almost gone. She could only read three things: *Rue des Jardins. Blue house. Big mango tree.* She kept it in her Bible. When I told her I was coming to Abidjan for my work, she gave it to me. She said: *If you have one free day, look for her.*"
Mamie takes the envelope. She recognizes her own handwriting. Her young handwriting, from 1979.
"Eleven years," she says. "This letter travelled for eleven years."
"And then thirty-six years more, to come back to you," says Sarah.
They both laugh. They laugh and cry at the same time, under the old palm tree, while the waves come and go.

Behind them, forty students, three teachers, two parents, Fatou and Junior are watching in total silence. Madame Diallo is wiping her eyes with a tissue. Ibrahim is pretending he has sand in his eyes.
Then Sarah takes out her phone.
"In London, it's the same time as here," she says. "Eleven o'clock. She's probably in her garden. Do you want to see her?"

Mamie looks at the phone. She looks at Aya. All week, Aya was angry at that little machine. The machine that kept her awake. The machine that made her fall in the road. The machine that took Fatou's nights.
But now Aya understands something. A phone is like a knife in Mamie's kitchen. You can cut okra for the sauce, or you can cut your finger. It depends on how you use it.
"Yes," says Aya to Sarah. "Please. Call her."
Sarah makes the video call. It rings. One time. Two times. Three times.
Then a face appears on the screen. An old woman with white hair, a straw hat and soil on her cheek. Behind her there are tomato plants and a grey English sky.
"Sarah, darling? Is everything all right? You look like you're crying!"
Sarah does not answer. She just turns the phone.
On the screen, Margaret sees a beach. A palm tree that leans towards the sea. And under the palm tree, a small woman in a blue dress with gold flowers.
For a long moment, nobody speaks. Not in London. Not in Grand-Bassam.
Then the woman in the blue dress says, softly:
"Thank you."
And the woman in the garden, with tears running down to her smile, answers:
"Merci."

They talk for one hour. In English, in French, in a mix of both, with many words they invent. Mamie shows Margaret her daughter, Mariam, who came with the bus at the last minute. Margaret shows Mamie a photo of her own daughter, Sarah's mother, a doctor in Manchester.
"*Your daughter and my daughter,*" says Margaret. "Do you remember? We wanted them to be friends."
"Our daughters were too slow," says Mamie. "But our granddaughters are fast."
She points at Aya and Sarah. Aya and Sarah look at each other and smile.

They make a new promise. Next year, Margaret will come to Grand-Bassam. Sarah will bring her. And they will all meet under the old palm tree. Margaret, Akissi, their daughters and their granddaughters. Three generations. One beach.
"This time," says Margaret, "we have telephones. Nobody will get lost."
Before they leave the beach, Aya and Sarah do something together. With a stick, in the wet sand under the palm tree, they write two names. The same two names that two other girls wrote in 1975.
**AKISSI** ♡ **MARGARET**
The waves come and take the letters away. But that's OK. Some things don't need to stay in the sand.

That night, back in the blue house in Yopougon, Aya lies on her bed. Her phone is on the table, with its cracked screen. She sends one message to Sarah: *Safe flight. See you next year under the palm tree.* She sends one message to Fatou: *Ice cream tomorrow? I pay. You pay.*
Then she puts the phone down, screen to the table.
Through the window, the moon is big and white and round. It is the same moon that shines over London. The same moon that shone over two girls on a beach in 1975.
Aya looks at it for a long time. And then, for the first time in a very long time, she falls asleep before midnight.
**THE END**

title: The Silent Week
author: Léxi
desc: Aya, 15 ans, perd son téléphone pendant une semaine à Yopougon… et découvre le secret de sa grand-mère.
